newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Banque Audi 1996 profits jump.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Banque Audi 1996 profits jump.

text.p: Lebanon's Banque Audi, whose shares have traded actively on the Beirut Stock Exchange since their introduction a week ago, on Monday reported a 52.5 percent rise in profits in 1996.
Assets, customer deposits, loans and equity also rose sharply, the bank said in its audited results for 1996.
Chairman Georges Audi, in a statement accompanying the results, described them as "very favourable."

Consolidated net profits for the bank and its fully-owned subsidiary Audi Investment Bank (Infibank) rose to 30.7 billion Lebanese pounds ($19.8 million) from 20.1 billion pounds in 1995, the statement said.
The 52.5 percent jump compared with a 57.7 percent increase in 1995.

Banque Audi has consolidated its position as one of Lebanon's top banks since the end of the 1975-90 civil war. It ranked third among Lebanon's 82 banks in assets and customer deposits in 1995 and fourth in size of loans.

In their first week of trading on the Beirut Stock Exchange, its shares rose to $15.875 from their January 20 opening price of $15. They have become the most active shares, helping to enliven a hitherto dull market.
The bank's statement said earnings per share rose in 1966 to $1.43 from $0.96 in 1995 and net return on average assets rose to 1.23 percent from 1.08 percent.
Other 1996 results included a 35 percent increase in assets, a 27.9 percent rise in customer deposits, and increases in loans and equity of 32 percent and 26 percent respectively.

In his statement, chairman Georges Audi noted that net profits rose faster (52.5 percent) than average assets (33.1 percent) and attributed the performance to asset liability management and interest rate management.

"The bank's consistent asset liability management and its rigorous interest rate management raised the net interest margin from 3.02 percent in 1995 to 3.50 percent in 1996, which lies at the roots of these very favourable 1996 performances," Audi said.

The bank's five-year, $100 million Eurobond issue in November 1996 significantly reinforced its funding sources and raised their average life above 170 days compared with a sector average of around 50 days, he said.
"The bonds, listed on the London Stock Exchange, are currently traded at around 103 7/8, which translates the good market perception of the bank's credit risk," Audi said.

Other 1996 developments, which included the launch of housing loans, the expansion of loans to small and medium enterprises and the bank's diversification into investment banking and private banking "will provide the main crux of the bank's growth over the coming years," Audi added.
